castItem.role: Henry VI., Emperor of Germany and King of Sicily.
William, Boy-pretender to the throne of Sicily.
Margaritone, Lord High Admiral of Sicily.
Peter de Celano, Minion to the Emperor.
Andrea, a Priest, afterwards a Monk, brother to Peter de Celano.
Adheld, German Page to Peter de Celano.
Constantia, Empress of Germany and Queen of Sicily.
Madeleine, sister to Adheld, in Iolante's train.
Azaire, a Moorish girl, waiting-woman to Iolante.

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: —Room in a Sicilian Palace. Enter Veronica and Margarito.

lg.l: The Emperor
Is then about to land?
And in his train
Are notable Sicilians.
Ay, indeed!
Markwald of Anweiler they say leads home
Iolante, our fair countrywoman.—Ah!
You fret your brow; my words I fear give pain;
Before the image of that saint I've marked
You're often on your knees. Your idol, sir,
Is now but rudely worshipp'd.
Will that make
Me less religious?
Your audacity
Becomes you, Margarito; 'tis the plume
Upon your cap.
I was at Algiers
When she consented. So think not, fair dame,
I shall be less her gallant when she comes
Once more to grace Palermo.—You will find
One worthy of your arts in Henry's train.
Oh! he will bring you one step from your throne
Who makes all women crouch!
Celano here?
I only love my countrymen, nor those
Among them who are leagued to give our land
To insufferable Teutons.
All the same
You'll catch him as the plague-spot; he exhales
An amorous infection. Henry's self
Is sick of him.
For this I prophesy
A pair of Teuton eyes whose northern blue
Shall freeze your patriotism. Nay, but here
We'll have no noisy politics. I've set
Those words to music; will you sing them now?
I think it was Sicilia that forgot.
Veronica, there's that within your voice—
You've known no heart-break; it must be a part
Of your superb dissimulation, yet
You earn this kiss—a tribute to your skill.
A hand—oh, it's not white!—a sonneteer
Could not express it. 'Tis too exquisite
For any use but this.
'Tis mine to give
In hospitality and to assure
Frank welcome to my guests.
Ah! I divine
You've been consulting with this lady how
Our too time-scanted city can prepare
For her great monarch's entry!
Surely you,
Who have put off your native manners, best
Can teach the taste of foreigners.
I will,
With promptest courtesy. You first must paint
These waxen cheeks a German would despise
As bloodless.
This is artifice to bring
The balsam-blushes to the lady's face.
In future it must be great Markwald's self,
As famed by sea as land in victories,
Must loiter in your galleries, and not
A sailor of your isle.
This insolence,
Save as enriching us with rainbow change,
From rose to pearl, were scarce deserving note.
Lady Veronica cannot forget
She is Sicilian,—doubtless she will give
To strangers welcome, be they German churls
(Crowds of Apulian captives in their train)
Or ...
Have you lover's right for this?
Now speak,
Veronica.
He simply has the right
Of subject to speak honour of his queen.
Am I to blame men seek me on their knees,
My dear lord councillor?
Superbly urged!
Now, sir, the hour of public audience
Is pass'd, I claim a lover's privacy,
My right; the lady has denied it yours.
State-business, not Veronica, forbids
A further parley.
Now be merciful.
Tell me of Andrea.
His sickness wanes.
If Heaven should restore him ...?
You would add
A pray'r I should release him to espouse
The girl Veronica, whom he seduced—
The girl who, when a virgin, won the heart
Of Peter de Celano:—so I will,
On this condition: it be noised abroad
How my young brother won your love before
You were my bride, and how you forced his mind.
Prepare your blushes.
I will do your will,
Beseeching only grace for Andrea.
I taught him earthly passion; he is pure—
As Mother Church could wish; he's penitent
Now of his frailty: to the holy nun
Who from his fever hath deliver'd him,
He's sworn the remnant of his life to pray'r
And patient fasting.
Penitent! Oh then,
I do beseech you marry me—
Not yet.
O God! It must be false; let me see words—
His hand.
“Veronica, I've found my bride,
The Church; 'twas only when you feign'd her voice
I loved you.”
Let me counsel! Your one aim
Must be to woo the brother in the world,
Still unespoused—to-morrow to contract
With Madeleine, a fair Thuringian
In Iolante's retinue:—and yet
I hesitate, for the young Moor Azaire
Hath turn'd upon me her black amorous eyes
With passion I had best assuage.
I am
Your victim; give me orders; but my name!
Have pity on it, if 'twill be your wife's.
Had you as wife betray'd me in this sort!—
As it is you'll suffer while I recollect.
Veronica!
Eyes blue as incensed air, and, oh! I thought
As holy; every drop that falls a gem.
Pooh! they're to mourn the Church's prisoner!
Not the lips!—but haply he o'erlook'd this brow.
I'll think it is Celano's. Keep it smooth.
I'll live for my good name. He only knows
My misery, and he will lighten it.
Margaritone shall not haunt my house.
What said he of a Moorish girl? Can I ...
Veronica,—can he put me to the shame
Of suffering a rival; must I wait
Till he's worn out a brace of victims, ere
I'm safe in all a wife's serenity?
My course is clear:—
He has ambition, and I'll cover it
With the mantle of my grace. We'll rule the world.

div.head: Scene II.
div.stage: —A Room in another Sicilian Palace. Iolante seated before a mirror; Azaire, herself crowned with roses, is wreathing her mistress's hair.

lg.l: How well these passionate red roses look
Against a skin the ardent sun hath kiss'd
Into a shame of darkness! On my white
The crimson hearts would pour their rich desire
And find it harshly virginal. Swart brows
Alone should carry roses. How say'st thou?
All lovers give them ...
Ah, you have a love?
Is he a Moor or a good Christian soul?
I may not tell. ... I know not anything.
You never have been awkward till in love;
But Love is blind, so we must give a hand
To help his stumbling. What a handkerchief
You've tied about your neck!—the needles sure
Stitch'd it with threads of the three heavenly skeins
That make a rainbow. You'll outshine the bride.
All joy and blessing be with you from Heaven.
But must a bride
Put by the roses of her blood and wear
Only the lilies of her spotless flesh?
Methinks Azaire
Hath stol'n your cheeks to set upon her brow.
My bridegroom loves another!
Let me go
To get ...
There's water in the ewer, child;
'Tis useless for the heart. My Madeleine,
One that could cut you to the quick of grief
Hath never loved you.
But the veil I'll keep
For spousal with my Christ.
O cruelty,
Wild beast of vices, sin with claw and tooth,
The heart thou holdest is a den, tho' hung
With grace as with a vine! Surely in jest
You have been wrong'd. Celano comes himself.
I come for my fair bride.
You've frightened her.
Her lips are trembling as a dove's two wings.
Press them to calm with kisses.
They are grey.
I'll close thy brown ones with a kisses together,
My nightingale!
What does this mean? Azaire,
Confess that you are guilty.
Yea, of love.
We were fellow-maids together, tho' you kept
The Moorish girl well hid. Last night unseen
I took a bunch of roses from his hand
For Madeleine; he kept mine prisoner,
And smiled, “The roses were a bridal-wreath,”
He bade me twist them in my hair, and wait
His pleasure till the morrow.
It is mine
That instantly you leave me, traitoress.
Retire in my protection. Mark ye that.
Hither, sweet slave.
'Tis not unmannerly
To ask for what pertains not to you now.
To Cæsar what is Cæsar's, to the bride
What is the bride's.
And what is God's to God.
May I have this veil in which to wed myself
To Heaven?
Nay, sister.
Then I'll dress your bride.
Th' attire is all about me. I shall want
No help. I am your humble maid, Azaire.
Less rigorous the service of my bride
Than that of Christ's.
Her servants must put on
Meekness as livery, and this event
Shall be the loom on which I'll weave it me,
For Christ's sake,
and for yours, Celano, yours.
Delay not then, fair maid, to dress the bride.
I had learnt the duties of a wife by rote,
The first obedience. With will as meek
As he had found in Madeleine his wife,
I veil Azaire.
Well spoken! we will wait
At the chapel, friends, with your good grace and leave.
Am I a creature of bed-ridden will
To suffer it?—And Madeleine is gone!—
Oh, good my lord, great treachery is here.
Celano hath but now departed hence
With Azaire as his bride, and Madeleine
Weeping behind, like Love's new year and old.
I know Celano's business everywhere,
But look not for him here, where I have peace
With Iolante.
But you do not note
His sin's enormity. He's broken troth
With one as stainless as the marble is,
O'er-fountain'd every moment, and—the shame!—
Hath grossly ta'en the Moorish girl.
In sooth,
I like not these alliances of blood
At natural enmity;—
But you, offend not Peter, for the king
Holds him in highest love. He wields the brain
O' the monarch; I but execute commands.
Loyalty, Iolante! Why this morn
My prince hath spoken of a marriage-tie
Between my sister Clara and the young
Sicilian Margarito.—Ah, he comes,
My future brother.
Trusting here to find
The maiden whom the Emperor makes my wife,
Your sister Clara.
Lady, have I leave
To rob you of the sweet companionship
Of those most grave blue eyes?
Get her consent,
And I will order Clara to appear.
The German maids are shy, but true of heart.
Believe you, you can trust her.
So we meet.
The little missal that you left with me,
And those slight rhymes you gave me to re-set,
I will return to you.

Nay, Margarito, they are no love-favours. Think not Clara will be jealous when she sees the holy prayers I tasked you with, or the childish words I prayed you bind into a canzonet. Clara will give the answer to my foolish wonder why love hath wings.
I did not ask for music.
True; but I
Needed it.
Margarito, I am vex'd
To hear you're taking Clara for your wife.
Oh, I have suffer'd from such nuptial news!
I fear you're yielding to your monarch's choice.
Teutons to licence press their loyalty;
But we Sicilians, we should mate for love.
Have you?
I was not chosen by the Emperor;
Scarcely in secret dare my Markwald woo,
Nor had he won the king's consent except
For his rare services.
Oh, I will make
Your Clara happy. We Sicilians,
We're masters in the art of catching love.
The woman is not born I could not make
Life-happy with my smile. Veronica,
The haughtiest beauty that Palmero boasts—
The silk rustles when I near her. Do you think
I'll fail to get the homage of that frank,
Little, stolid-hearted Teuton?
What, you brag?
Margaritone, for this haughtiness
May Cupid humble you! In turn confess
Where pay you homage?
To my countrymen—
That is, excluding males. You're for the feast
The king holds on the day our little prince
Must give away his crown—a pretty sight—
For title of a count? You will be there
To see this, Iolante?
How escape?
Tis my lord's office to pick up the crown
And offer it to Henry; it is mine
In all fair ceremonies by his side
To stay assenting.
To my music, then!
I've had a task
To bring her hither. When you're at the wars
You'll leave her safely; she will keep the house.
And I will keep her heart—a precious charge.
Clara—O eyes blue as the sea I love!—
Will you come teach me of Teutonic faith,
And give the wild sea-captain a sure port
To anchor in, when life's tempestuous?
If you are friendly to my land.
A fleet
At th' Emperor's service is my warranty.
If so—why then ...
What is the rest, my lord?
Sweet Clara, this—that you must be my wife.
Tears!
You're a stranger.
Dear, of course I am.
Would you marry with your brother!
That's well urged.
Come, come, I'll take you to your sovereign lord,
And when you know it is his will you wed,
You will not close your fist against the ring.
Can such a nature pour into a creek?
Ay, but it washes the whole world beside.
'Tis hot, an air for roses, not for men.
What were we saying?
Please you, my good praise,
Which made the summer hotter on my cheek.
True, Peter, you're the apple of our eye;
The perfect politician; but this whim
Of setting in a Moorish wench's train
A lady of our land ...
For discipline;
I'd have a wife the Sultan could not match,
Amorously dull—no treason. I would sleep
On's knee, and dream what beauties I desire;
She watching till she snored.
Well, let us hear
Of the Moor's speedy death. Your gallantries
Outrage our honest German court. Don't take
Your wickedness to church. A monstrous freak,
To play the bridegroom to that devil-born
Hot-blooded little beauty.
Absolute
Your will as my obedience.
There strikes
The hour we granted Markwald.
Fool, you here?
Surely when wisdom goes out of door, folly may peep in at window.
Has a fool eyes?
No; coupled with Love, he's blind.
That most melancholy man, the Archbishop, has found you gamesome.
I feed on him, he's victuals to me; he's so desperate a man, and a pride—oh, but I'd live to drive the waggon, with him at the cart's tail!
You shall.
Heyday, you humour me;—then hang him up by the leg and moralize. I'd preach to him by the hour.
You shall.

An' yet to see the poor man pull a long face, and convince him only by smiling could he hope to stand on two legs—to propose to him either to dimple his cheeks with laughter or his neck with the noose; all the time he fixing his dull fish eye upon me till it glazed. It were a spectacle!
He shall. The Archbishop walks much a' nights on the long terrace by the chestnuts. Lie on the wall and listen. Keep your ears prick'd for treason.
I'll be tale-bearer,
To see th' Archbishop hanging by the leg,
His long face downward! Ha, ha, ha!
You shall.

div.head: Scene IV.

lg.l: My Clara, comfort me. I have no maids
About me now; my bright Azaire is gone,
With her pretty Moorish ways, and Madeleine,
So sweet a preacher to my playfulness,—
For, Clare, I must be playful. Oh, I feel
A loneliness upon me, even here
In Sicily half-exiled.
Can that be
With Markwald's sister for companion?—but
I've seen you yawn in Markwald's company.
He's good enough for the king.
And yet for Iolante's veins too slow.
A child, I laugh'd and clapp'd my hands beside
The rivers that ran swift; the sluggish streams—
Iolante! These are most disloyal words.
I trust you feel some rev'rence for a name
The Emperor holds in honour.
Ay, and you,
You girl with the grave face, I trust you feel
A proper reverence
For the Lord High Admiral, who has, at best,
For the great Empire that you venerate
But politic affection?
Do you doubt?
Come now, I have you! Do you love this man
Better than your own German land and tongue?
Will you forget them all, and with his kiss
Receive Sicilia to your heart?
Oh no!
My brother wishes me to marry him—
And, and ...
That massy raven hair framing a brow
Of stainless marble! Clare, I often think
With men, like Margarito, who have lives
Fulfill'd of knightly enterprise, the tears
They have no time to shed, soften the clime
O' the eyes to exquisite humidity.
Clare, did you see how as he turn'd he gave
His life away with one glance of his eyes?
He's right to trust me so; we German girls
Are never treach'rous.
The wise brother Mark,
For all your bitter words, has shown no fear
Of a Sicilian bride.
Who slanders him
Behind his back.
Most virulently:—not my lord alone.
'Tis natural
In me, removed from anything I love,
To eye in the cold blood of commentary
Its virtues and defects. My Markwald's voice
Makes me again a partisan. But, Clare,
You think I love you is a spell to keep
Margaritone at your side? I say
He'll need to be cajoled, implored, malign'd,
Threaten'd, entreated twenty times a day
To keep in temper;—more, to be amused,
As to his head, sweet Clara, by your wit.
Can you listen to his sonnets? Shall you care
Hear of his Arab training? In a word,
Can you dish up this crude sincerity
Into a pretty falseness without guile?
Never; that is your way.
Go, sullen girl!
But when you're mew'd up with your tapestry,
Your lord a-hunting, sick of his dull home,
You'll cease to blame
Your sister Iolante: you will know
She's the wise matron who, when truth's a thorn,
Mosses it o'er with falsehood for the feet
She loves to tread on.—I was saying, dear,
She knows not how to rule my countrymen.
She says
Sincerity is crude; moss it with lies
For lovers' footsteps.
Iolante! Wife!
Thus he expostulates!—But why this brow
So over-clouded?
Women's tears, they rust
The blade of manhood! I have stood two hours
By the old stricken queen, who on her knees
Beseeches Henry to return her child,
When he's discrown'd him. “'Tis himself I want;
His breath, his hair, his limbs.” She supplicates—
“Take all his royalties.”
There is no way?
My lord is stark; she must resign the child
Into his charge.
Oh, he's too mere a babe
For men to handle.
Could you nurture him
Till he's of age for convent discipline—
For he must be a priest—my lord might yield,
As you're my wife. He knows our loyalty.
Why Iolante would so love the boy
She'd join in a conspiracy to put
The crown on 's head.
Foul slander, Clare; she trusts
Her husband so entirely she would give
The children of her body to be torn
Piecemeal if he required it. If I win
This favour, you must show a great reserve
To Margarito and Sybilla.
Yes.
For the rest mother, I could no more face
Such spoil of nature than frequent the streets
Of a sack'd town; but Margarito, think!—
Whom Clare will soon becloud, we must not keep
His spirits on low diet, or the king
Will dream he's plotting treasons. She's too slow
For a Sicilian.
From experience
You speak?—
Yes, Markwald, you can't understand
Half that I fell:—for Sicily,
Sybilla, Margarito, even you,
Not half the ways I love you.

div.stage: [She puts up her hands to caress him; as he pushes them back, a joint of his armour grazes one of them.

lg.l: You must learn
Not fight against my will when I command.
You think yourself too clever; I must keep
My wife from peril.—What, you are not hurt?
It's nothing.
A mere scratch; but such may break
The skin of the spirit. You'll not rule me thus.
Leave me awhile.
Iolante, I am come
To have you teach me how to court my love.
She's obstinate.
Then try the Teuton way.
Drive your affection as with hammer in
The soft places of her heart.
I did not know
I broke upon your privacy.
You do.
At present for state reasons 'tis my wish
That you be little at my house; my wife,
I trust, may have Prince William in her charge
To teach the German language.
I obey,
Most grateful for the cause; intelligent
Of your prudent fear and forethought.
There you judge
Most circumspectly. I'll unfold you more.
I would befriend Sicilia.
He is gone.
Before a stranger I've insulted him,
My Markwald! I have given him no son,
And he a child of my own race to rear.—
I'll sue for grace in Margarito's sight.
Margarito!—Oh, my lord!
Thanks, on my knees,
For your great gift and pardon! When you say
In our Sicilian, which you blunder at,
A word too strong, I put it back again
In your own speech more gentle—so I sought
To turn you from a course that seem'd more stern
Than I with wifely privilege descry
The purpose of your heart.
Iolante, God hath given us no child.
I thought the boy would comfort you.
He will—
Not only as Sicilian, as your gift.
Oh, Markwald ...
There, there! Why the merest touch
Of a mail'd hand brings blood to a woman's cheek.
Kneeling for pardon! Love, a German wife
Could not look humbler in her penitence,
Nor half so handsome.
End as you began—
Wife, Iolante!
Iolante, wife.

div.head: Scene V.
div.stage: —Celano's House. A Room. Enter Madeleine and Azaire.

lg.l: It grieves me sore
Thus to receive your service.
'Tis his will
And Heav'n's. I, humbling thus myself, shall win
High place in paradise. Your beauty is
A snare to him.
Is 't that? I cannot tell.
I love him, Madeleine. It seems to me
That other women cannot look on Love
Save it be dress'd for them a thousand ways.
My appetite can diet on raw meat.
You love because 'tis profitable; Christ
Will think of your humility; while I
Love simply, madly, as I love the food
In sight when I am hungry. 'Twas a whim
That set the veil on me; but if instead
You had been honour'd, and my only hope
Of being loved by him a life of shame,
I would have stoop'd to 't. If I could not be
The silver flagon for his lips at feast,
Then the horn-cup he'd catch up for a drink
When he was thirsty, hunting. So I love.
I do not care for anything but love,
Nor how I get it. He is coming in.
You'll leave us, Madeleine.
My lord forbids
That I should ever leave you. I'll retire
In shadow to my tapestry.
How cold
The girl is! I could hate her.
Well, Azaire,
My little spit-fire wife, what angers you?
I'm vex'd and angry at this misery.
Remove it from me ere I kiss you.
See,
My pretty tyrant, how your slave obeys.
Madeleine, leave us.
There!—How lovelier
You look each hour, a rose-bud that at dawn
Was only a red rose-bud and to-night
Bends over me all rose, even to the air
It breathes on me. Say, are you wholly mine?
In the whole world do you love aught but me?
You're all to me. One language and one life
Are far too short for me to reckon up
My wealth in you.
Do you love God?
Oh no!
Not in the least; remove that jealousy.
Why that is well; then you are wholly mine.
No, you are mine, mine own.
Yours, little fool!
Ay, as a wine-butt is sole property
O' the cup. I am the world's.
Oh, misery!
You love none save Azaire?
I woo a dame
Who pray'd me on her knees to marry her.
She loves you?
No. Why is it that you love?
Tell me, Azaire.
You're beautiful; your voice
Is like a touch to me, your touch a bond.
None ever loved Celano in this sort.
And does Celano love that other one
So, thus?
What, Madeleine?
That girl who asks?
You mean your servant. No, child; but the king
Compels me to receive the icy girl
In my reluctant arms.
Then must I die.
O you delicious creature, no reproach!
Flee from me, sorceress! Among the hills
I have a tiny villa. There I'll come;
Nay, do not bind me—not a pledge. You know
You are the only woman in whose love
I have delight. You love so senselessly
You satisfy my soul. No tears! You start
At dawn; till then we'll make the darkness glad.

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: —A Window-seat in a Chamber of the Palace.

lg.l: O Iolante, was not that an owl
I' the sun-basking ivy? Yet forsooth,
The shadow of Time's finger points the noon,
Saw we a dial. Wherefore then this owl,
This hooded thing on the bright glove of day,
This page of purblind Night, this trumpeter
To tongueless apparitions?
'Tis to prick
Our joy with sense of mutability.
Did you not smile, your answer had been sad.
Ah me!
There's even such a rueful prophet lurks
Behind my branching gladness.
'Tis to make
More precious your felicity.
False cheer!
Obscure Distrust sits in my joy's recess,
Distrust, O Iolante, of my lord.
I've laid Sicilia in his grasp. To see
A mail'd hand close over a butterfly
Were not more cruel. Ah, there was a time
I could have mated you! But then he came,
Th' Apulian Conqueror, and gave my sweet'st
Companion to his stalwart captain ere
My lips recover'd liberty. And I
Must bear him children, as my countrymen
Yield him their labour's first-fruits. My desire
Is not to make him father; 'tis to give
A man-child to my country. O my land,
My life, my blood, for thee my womb's in toil,
And I shall see thy prince's heritage
Trampled before my face; Sicilian blood
Pour'd out by him who hath begot my child.
This is distraction.
Such distraction waits
On motherhood, my queen; full treasuries
Bring terrors and forebodings of the thief;
Pangs that the poor
Would suffer smiling. Were I in your case,
Sweet lady, I would bear your world of cares
To feel a babe's hand patter its soft praise
O' my bosom's bounty. But you err to think
My monarch forced me into marriage-bonds.
I love the good duke Markwald; openly,
With all the noblest of my land in sight,
I must have chosen him; he's true of heart,
Most stern for justice.
Iolante, say—
Do you love best your country or your lord?
My lord so well that I have given him
Even to his charge my Sicily in trust.
Oh, Iolante, I abide at home
And will not see plots brewing,—will not see
Old playmates in mask'd faces greeting me.
A shadowy headsman ever is behind;
While Henry keeps
Close lips and moves about with courtesy.
There's thunder in his nature.
A sweet son
Will soften him. The Hohenstaufen hair,
Keep to the golden tinct.
My southern blood
Repels invasion from the north; my child
Will be all Sicily. Unhappy boy,
A poet-hearted prince, set i' the midst
Of barbarous Teutons—Iolante! What!
Are you asleep?—Almost. The very time,
Still with satiety of light and heat,
Is Slumber's opportunity. Lie here;
Do as your eyes would have you, for their lids
Are curving to half-moons.
And leave the queen
Untended!
Others with more wakeful orbs
Shall dress me for the council, which my lord
Untimely holds at mid-day. Sicily
Is on her knees that I should slumber not.
The halcyon Sleep
Hath made a blessed calm. O safest hour
To turn her with the helm of my desire
From anchor'd port to Love's free waves. But if
She will not swerve?—why, then there is the make
O' the brute in Markwald; if I madden him,
He'll so be-tyrant her, she'll take my course;
She's the prow-head of my spirit.—What! My glove!
I'll leave it here for Markwald to surmise
His worst; my longings far outleap his fears.
I'll kiss her for an earnest of my guilt.
Iolante, I'm audacious. I'll awake
And daze her with the glare of my wild love.
My Iolante!
Where's Margarito?—What a cry is this?—
From such assault
Your sword, my knight, should save me. Slay the beast
Who with vile purpose hath surprised my couch.
I must be satisfied ...
I'm safe; scarce knew I, waking suddenly,
What had befallen. Heaven give me strength
To rescue him from peril.—Why to-night
I'll yield to your entreaties; we'll cajole
The unsuspecting Teuton; he shall learn
What it is to trust Sicilians.—You are cold;
You do not answer me.
Oh horrible
To catch Lust's accents on those holy lips!
The fair saint Iolante I'd seduce;
Not a base creature who would tempt me with
Suggestion fouler than my devilish thought.
The solemn Clara shall be mock'd—
Peace, peace!
It is as God's own mother from her shrine
Should stoop to tempt and cozen. I'll away
From this cursed Sicily; all patriot thought
I'll smother and resign myself
To any life of blasphemy: what hope
If Iolante is ...
There is no hope
For any land whose women dare not trust
Their countrymen. I, in Sicilia's name,
Appeal to you. From holy sleep I woke
To find you in temptation. Heav'n hath heard,
Camping the legion'd angels round your soul,
Ere my slow prayers could mount. Confess yourself
At chapel, Margarito. Do not think
Of Clara till you're shriven.
And of you
Never? You set a gulf
'Twixt my damn'd exile and your blessedness?
I'll bridge it an unhallow'd way ...

sp.speaker: Iolante.

lg.l: I trust
The man who not a moment could delight
In woman thought disloyal. From henceforth
I trust you wholly, Margarito. But,
Since noble Markwald's sister hath a heart
Like her brother's of true temper, I must train
Your ill-deserving spirit to receive
The worship of such natures. Fare you well.

sp.stage: [Giving her hand, which he kisses reverently.

lg.l: What is there in me brings the devils thick
As flies to honey? Is it possible
A knight could fall to lust of anything
That has no smutch of sin? At church I've seen
A picture of lean Lust; she dieted
On refuse. Faugh!
I am not beautiful
Th' ensnaring way. My simple netted hair
It's wavy brown and only good enough
For the wind to play with; and my skin is clear;
My Markwald says I have a homely cheek
For an honest man to kiss; and any child
Has eyes like these. Veronica 's a throat
One needs must gaze on as the dazzling wall
Faced with chalcedony; mine's common stone.
My wife before a mirror! Vanity!
Markwald, what do you see here?

sp.speaker: Markwald.

lg.l: Not a saint,
And by no means a beauty; not a flow'r,
Nor jewel; but a pretty little girl,
Who'll sing and smile and not forget her pray'rs
For one she loves;—a little thing to trust.

sp.stage: [She silently embraces him and goes out.

lg.l: She kiss'd me sobbing; she is not herself.
What's yonder?—Margarito's glove!—The fool 's
Been telling her she's handsome: my poor praise
Doubtless fell flat. I will not suffer him
About my wife. Iolante!
What is this?
A glove. 'Twas Margarito let it drop;
He has been with me, had been with me now
But that I sent him to confession: he
Displeased me much.
Confess to me the sin
You sent him to the priest with.
What, betray!
Shall a priest's ear
Be safer than a lady's breast? My lord,
No curious torture could wring out from me
The least
Of the words you woo'd me with: they're buried here
'Mong other precious relics: rifle not!
What's laid on the altar 's consecrate, altho'
It be not my lord Markwald's offering.

div.stage: [Curtsies, playfully shakes her head, and retires.

lg.l: I like it not; yet could as lief accuse
A child of treason as that face of thought
Un-innocent. Some grief of her country's perhaps
With which he pester'd her. Poor child, she loves
Her Sicily, and I must execute
My king's commands, discrown her little prince
To-morrow. It will cut her to the heart.

div.head: Scene II.
div.stage: —Room of State. Enter with great pomp the Emperor, the Empress, Prince William, Markwald, Celano, Margarito, Sybilla, Iolante, Veronica, and others.

lg.l: My Germans and Sicilians, whom the cloak
Of empire would enfold—my equal care,
To-day we take our lawful sovereignties
From the thief's hand, glad that his tender years
So plead for him, we can preserve his life.
His ancestors—
Curse him, ye dead!
Have brought
The fair boy to this day's disgrace; he stands
Bringing the colour to Sicilian cheeks
At thought of their misplacèd fealty—
Curse him, ye living!
For the guilt of birth
Desiring pardon: eager to protest
His parents did most wrongfully usurp
My southern throne.

sp.speaker: Sybilla

lg.l: O God the Father, curse!
Come hither, child.

sp.stage: [As he comes to her, she thrusts him forward, and looks up to heaven, then glances at the Emperor.]

lg.l: Curse him, O Christ the Son.
He doth not cry; his face is like a cloud
That holds the rain.
Come, little lord, step up.
Come hither.
Bravo!
Kneel, and speak by me.

I, William, unlawfully called of Sicily king, do here on my knees tender to my liege-lord Henry— Emperor—the crown and lands which are his, to hold and have; beseeching mercy for the great sin of their treasonous retention by me and my fathers committed against God and our liege-lord, whose hand I kiss and tremble.
It is not thunder, but Sicilia's groan.
Rise, Count of Lecce,—rightful title this,
Which sons may bear—a spotless heritage.
Our dearest vassal, our henceforward joy!
Sicilians, see! our knees are Mercy's throne.
The golden light hath tasted misery
In the bow'd sunshine of that golden head,
That leaves our hearts in night.
Oh, do not speak!
Yet since on stock of rude disloyalty
We would engraft obedience, this boy,
From the accustom'd care of his own kin
We take, to give him, underneath our eye,
New cherishing and foster discipline,
Entrusted to staunch Markwald and his wife.
Sire, we are honour'd servants—Come to her.
Maria—Mother! Curse the barren thing
Whose womb was never thrill'd nor bosom suck'd,
To whom they give the child that I have borne.
Willie!—my little ...
His tears within us blush to drops of blood
We'll weep in battle.
Cover up your fires,
Friend Admiral.
There, there! We'll go away.—
I'll take him to my little privy bow'r,
Wherein the honied woodbine's dainty paps
Suckle the bees, and tell him fairy-tales.
You've stripp'd me of my child; 'twere modesty
To hide my naked motherhood.
Yes, yes.
We spare your presence.—Take her from the hall.
Rejoice, Sicilians, for your lawful queen
Will speedily present you with a prince
Worthy your homage. Stay, Constantia, stay,
Smile on your people and confirm their hope.
I'm deadly faint.

sp.speaker: Emperor.

lg.l: You'll be obedient;
'Tis the ex-queen retires.

sp.stage: [Taking her hand, he presents her to the people.

lg.l: See, she descends
To mingle with you and receive your loves.
Thus intermarried
we shall breed a race
Will overcome the world.

div.stage: [Exeunt all save Margarito and the Archbishop of Salerno.

lg.l: You lag.
He will not reach the ships till noon.
I entertain him there.
You note he pass'd
Betwixt two rows of corpses to the feast—
His queen look'd not more ghastly.
I've the fleet.
Those lords
I'll answer for. Can you contrive
To visit them and preach submission
To their new earthly lord?
I'll stir their blood.
That boy I wash'd in baptism, and now
Have stain'd the royal roses of his lips
With fond self-slander and base perjury.
We yet will teach them truth! No whispering,
No nervous penitence; be affable;
This is a holiday: go you to church;
Welcome your monarch to its shrine. To-night
You shall confess me as the clock strikes twelve.

sp.speaker: Veronica.

lg.l: Come hither, Adheld. You're my lord's fair squire.

sp.stage: [He kneels and presents a letter from Celano.

lg.l: What think you of his service, sweetest boy?
So highly do I rate him, lady, all
He does I imitate; what he admires
I find most admirable; where he bows
In worship, I more reverently kneel.
He teaches me religion; 'tis thro' him
Mine eye drinks in divinity.
In sooth!
Oh, these are pretty speeches in a boy.
Is 't to your taste—
Yes, fan me!—that your sister acts the part
Of servant to a Moor? Now, sweet young face,
Be frank.
My lord by Cæsar hath been urged
To right this strangest injury:—my blood
Not long will bear the insults that are heap'd
On Madeleine.
We women of the world
Can but confess to utter innocence.
I'm going now
To be familiar with you, as a child
I should take up, and sob upon his neck;
Such trust I have in you.
'Tis too much grace.
Doth the Virgin tell in Heaven what she hears
Betwixt the warm veil'd lips and Ave-sighs?
I know she's secret. I have faith in you.
You'll hear, and you'll obey me, for you love.
My squire, I'll make you perfect in Love's arts,
And when they're yours, I'll smile to see them used
On some sweet girl I mother'd at the font.
Incredulous! Ah!—You'll obey my words?
As my lord's orders.
Then you'll never let
Your sister fall, not even as a bride,
Prey to the dread Celano. Get her housed
Safe in a nunnery. My heart implores.
I am his victim; he refuses me
The one name that can right me. Help me,—ho!
Sweet holy Adheld as thou hop'st to take
The vows of knighthood: 'tis for my good name
I seek to be Celano's wife, the while,
Adheld, I shudder at his proffer'd love.
Lady, you thrill such passion thro' my soul
That if it be your will the poison-draught
Should follow marriage, I am cup-bearer.
All, all that wrongs you is my enemy.
Fair child, forget this tragedy; be gay.
Serve me as you have opportunity.
Fail not to tell Celano how I droop,
A plant in darkness, wither'd for his sun.
I teach you no deception—falter not.
And do not miss to wait on me each day,
For comfort's sake of your pure morning face.
I give him but the irony of truth.
My hair is silv'ring fast. He'll win for me
The bridal crown before this amorous wealth
Is meagre. How I win men with a smile!
The purest sees my sorrow, not my sin.
Andrea will be the Church's saint; at least
Seduced Veronica shall take her place
'Mong holy matrons.—I am bidden forth.
Celano holds a dance within his halls.

div.head: Scene IV.
div.stage: —A Council-chamber. Enter Emperor, Celano, Markwald, and others.

lg.l: There's thunder in the air; the chargèd wrath
Best burst from us! Misdoubt me not; I smelt
The sulphur in the first Sicilian breeze;
When Margarito at the water's edge
Received us with so infinite a grace,
I mark'd him—an indomitable eye!
We put that sort of pris'ner to the sword,
Or we should never nap upon our throne
When we are sleepy. That's an eye to quench.
You wrong him, Sire; he's a true gentleman
Of bounteous nature.
So you warranted.
We had not else suffer'd our noble Clare
To be affianced to him.
Confidence
Hath a weak ankle, and the veriest stone
Of adverse circumstance may trip it up.
Let's test Margaritone ere we trust.
He's amorous and free of tongue; your wife
Sicilian, and in wisely courage safe.
Let them be close; if treason's in the land,
She'll give it us, the native accent pure.
Good; for this peace rots as a pestilence.
But if the gallant lady find no plot?
We'll hatch one.
Set your brains to work, and have
Your creatures ready, for I'm sick to death
Playing the part
Of feast-drowsed monarch, when I'm warn'd sharp steel
Is wanted: give me pretext and I'll strike.
Patience, my liege: Justice they say is blind,
Impartial and not hood-winked.
Set your dame
To play the pining patriot.
I will.
As she is my true wife, her single aim
Will be her king's security.
You smile?
Ha! ha!
The woman is not born will see such throat
Disparted from such shoulders.
I'm content
With the policy in train: thanks, gentlemen.

div.head: Scene V.
div.stage: —A Room in Celano's House. Madeleine working a veil; she pauses and looks at a picture on the wall.

lg.l: I thought it was Celano in his youth before he saw the world. He tells me 'tis his brother—still 'tis very like. I wonder where is the difference! I see—this lacks the funny lines about the mouth, and the eyes have not the polish. I want to pray to this picture as to a Saint Sebastian. I drop a bead a moment for Celano's soul. No one else but Madeleine would have patience to pray him into peace again. Since that wedding-day have I slept an hour? Yet when he's penitent he'll look like this. He has the smile—and there's such a landscape in his face to light when he throws the sun on it!
Dear brother!
Where's your mistress?

Gone to the coast, and, Adheld, she returns no more. Celano promised me when he came back from lifting her on her horse she should not return; so your quarrel with my lord is ended, and your sister—see!—is working for her bridal.
While the last bride is throttled by assassins.
Peace, brother! you forget we are betroth'd. Palermo looks on me as an injured wife.

If betrothal hold you, there's a lady to whom Celano was betroth'd as you say, ere he mimick'd love in your eyes—a lady whom, by force or some vile sorcery, he hath dishonour'd and keeps shame-gagg'd in her misery.
Some beauty that tempted:—he's not betroth'd.

Little tortoise-skull! how is it with your heart? Can one tread on it and leave no stain on the foot? Toss it to yon villains paving the street! I tell you, had you any faith or charity, you'd refuse him, take that veil, and give yourself to Christ.
I cannot think—

True, you fat flesh-heap! If Celano gave you a piece of gold and show'd you the very blood that purchased it, you'd say he got it honestly. I tell you, as Celano is my master, I serve him; but you, as you are Heaven's bond-maid, must disown him. He comes. Madeleine, work my will in this.
Well, Madeleine, what says the boy to you?
He wishes me to take the veil.
Oh, then
Tis lightly done. I loose you from the bond
Of my pre-contract with you.
You consent?
I do not force you; since the Emperor
Takes int'rest in you, I consult his will;
And if it be that I should marry you,
I shall do 't as I should take a city; if
Meanwhile you do not wed yourself to Heaven.
You ask a vessel, would it profit her
Remove the helm and with a childish crew
Drift on the waves! Give my unguided life
Your merciful direction.
Madeleine,
To-day I'm busy. Tell me what that boy
Was urging on you: be obedient.
He said you'd wrong'd a lady who desired
That you should wed her; and he threaten'd me
Because of that I should not be your wife.
Call Adheld—and you, tell your rosary.
If you like, listen. Adheld, you have kiss'd
Veronica's fair hand and felt the dew
Of her most excellent tears across her cheek.
You're ripe to poison me at her command.
Nay, blush not; I read clear; all's fair in love.
It is an arrant sorceress! My boy,
You think I've wrong'd her. Look upon that face,
Or cross the street and ask for Andrea
The priest who tends yon altar. Learn of him
Who to dishonour brought the stateliest girl
Man ever worshipp'd. I, my Adheld, sought
To wed her, and she mock'd me.
Dear my lord,
It was her modesty; she could not speak
The past; she's clear! So look the saints whose robes
Are dyed in blood; she'd stain her purity
With penitential tears.
Poor child, you're snared.
You'd strive to force me wed the loveliest bride
Sicilia ever grew her myrtles for.
Your artifice I smile at. Madeleine,
Will you be sway'd by me, or ...
I am yours—
I was. You never were betroth'd to her—
Lady Veronica?
Then we'll not fix
The day of your espousal—to the Lord?
Have you no pity? May your hard heart rot
Each day by morsels. Dear my lord have grace,
Give to the great Veronica the hand
Alone can hold her from abysmal shame.
Adheld, my honourable sentiments
To your sister half deter me.
Do not call
So mean a thing my sister! Of my blood
She is not, but a slave to her own lust.
Pray for me, Madeleine.

He looks to me for salvation. My duty is plain; this veil must be his bride's to save him from the snare of the evil woman. I will pray for him till my tongue swoons! Oh, what peril to him from the creature who could stain the innocence of the Church's holy son. Thank Heaven, I'm fast betroth'd. I'll leave this vanity
to pray him white as he was ere he went to court
A very seraph's brow!
A damnèd monk!
Iolante, 'tis my wish that you to-day
Greet Margarito, for whom Clara sighs,
And let him see young William; note his mood,
If with the sight it alter.
This is strange;
You banish'd Margarito from your house.
Orders are now reversed. You are not glad
Again to be his hostess?
Not his spy.
It is unworthy of you, dear my lord,
To put your Iolante to such use,
That you no more can teach her to fulfil
Than train an innocent, glad singing-bird
Hawk-wise to fix and fasten on its prey.
You keep your Iolante for delight
I' the music that she makes you; not at all
To loose from wrist that she may bear you back
The quarry of your bleeding enemies.
Is Margarito then an enemy?
Of whom?—the Emperor?
He comes. Obey.
What means my lord to put me in this strait?
They bring the boy: he shall not look on him;
There's that in 's face must grow to royalty,
And it might tempt ...
Mutter!
A German word!
So good at learning!—There, sweet boy, enough!
I'm sick to-day, and cannot stay to spell
The bright page of the missal: to the priest!
He's found the child—I catch the tenderness
Of voice. We will not speak of him at all.
Iolante, are you here alone?—in tears?
Sybilla ...
Not Sybilla, Sicily
Forgets the child she bore.
I'm Markwald's wife—
Even regret is treason in report.
In mine ear's treasury whate'er is cast
Is wealth my lord distributes at his will.
You tell me that in the Sicilian tongue?
What, use it as a traitor?
Not so grave!
Wives forget every bond when once they wear
This pledge—
Oh, tell me—do our slaves in chains
So forget freedom?—Iolante, say,
Why am I summon'd?
My lord summon'd you;
For what I know not.
And can scarce devise
A hasty welcome.—What is that you do?
A shirt I'm making for my foster-child.
These cares are new to me, and cost some tears,
For I am sonless, and my pretty guest
Is going to a convent.
What! your prince?
Tush, tush!
It's the child I'm thinking of; so delicate!
He's rooted in my heart; transplanting him,
So frail a slip, to rougher Earth—
Look there!
The child, who owns that:—all that jewelry
Of sea, the shining marble of these roofs,
Iolante, is preparing for the cowl?
Stay! With what fix'd eyes they are looking down
On the city! How he turns to make appeal!
Markwald, pass on: you know she'll tell you all.
Distrust me, I beseech—I must report—
Sweet patriot, do not so belie yourself.
I swear to you I will be ever true
To noble Markwald; you, I straight dismiss
For daring utter to me words no wife
Must listen to:—this is the only lie
To save betrayal. Go!
Have you obey'd?
My lord, I've wholly fail'd to play my part.
Margaritone has a lover's way;
And, ere we enter'd into grave discourse,
He put into his gestures and his tones
What well I know my Markwald would not like,
So I have straight dismiss'd him.
When you stood
Together, looking at the city, then
Were you dismissing him?
Even then in thought.
I did not summon him. I cannot play
The spy—be mask'd to my old friends. My lord,
Christmas is coming on, and the great feast
For which I am not able. Let me go
To our little sea-side villa. There I'll stay
Where I can bring no harm to those I love.
Who are they, Iolante?
You, my lord;
Margaritone as a countryman—
The child, all these. I have a parting charge
To make to you: trust, trust the Admiral
In all state matters, and beware of him
As rival. I'm o'er-scrupulous. You think
A married woman must not hear a word
Of praise from any but her lord. I won't.
So pray you put me beyond reach; for here
I must be much where my young countryman
Frequents—
Capricious fancy! Well then, go ...
And I must keep the feast without my wife.
Your talk was then of personal affairs?
Yes!—
Clare shall go.
Margaritone sure
Will seek to see her. I must be alone.
Leave Clara here.
The man is doom'd.—No, no.
You'll go together. I will see you start
This afternoon. There's myst'ry in my wife;
I would she had my sister's honesty!

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: —Room in a little lonely Villa. Andrea pacing up and down.

sp.speaker: Andrea.

lg.l: I am bidden here
To one of his poor victims. Should he ask
My priestly aid, I must confess him, yea,
Wash from his soul the spots I'd have hell-fires
Burn deep to ingrain'd devil. I must hear
Of amorous encounters, while my hands
Clutch the cold crucifix; mine unpurged blood
Will leap responsive to the sin my lips
Scourge with prescription of unnumber'd pray'rs.
Oh yet
There was a whiteness and a glory in
My way of ruin. On the rosary
I tell the minutes of that sacred hour.
My lady stoop'd
To teach me love, as she had taught a child
The missal's pages; since, illiterate,
The gold and crimson story would be lost
To eyes so bright with wonder.—Ah, she comes!

sp.stage: [Enter Azaire, pale, with a child in her arms.]

lg.l: A temptress beauty, no Madonna, tho'
She clasps a glorious babe.
He promised me
You would be kind, you are his brother—this,
This child, I bring for baptism his son;
And I wed to him in the open church
'Mid lords and ladies! Fair Veronica
Was there. I am his wife. I cannot live
Without him. The last parting broke my heart.
And he must keep away. I think he's dear
To the pale, waxen, proud Veronica,
Tho' now the Emperor forces him to wed
The German girl he was betroth'd to first.
He has been good
To me; he loves me, and he'll own his child.
They say you are his brother, sir.
I am.
Your boy shall be baptized. What name?
My babe!
I have no will; he call'd thee. Andrea,
See that his father loves him; take the child.
Will you not shrive you, if so soon to die?
I am a Moor.
Oh, let me speak to you
Of Christ and His great sorrows; you will burn
In hell if thus you die.—
Thus—loving dear
My husband and my child?
Nay, in your sins.
Have you no hate
Of that proud dame Veronica? You say
She loves your husband?
I don't think of her
In anger; me he loves—poor chrysalid,
What is my worth now? Those the crimson wings
The glory of my nature went to fledge!
Azaire shall live in her man-child. Oh, say
I travel southward toward a deeper sun—
I die of thirst and hunger—thirst for love
And hunger for my child. Oh, tell my lord
The Moorish girl is dying in the sun.
He'll see her eyes again in the dark boy
She bore him; let him love the young Azaire!

div.stage: [Lays the child at his feet; as he raises it, she turns back, stretches her arms to it, and rushes out.

lg.l: What mockery!
Our Andrea had sprung from gentlest blood—
The tiny waxen figure put to sleep
On a nun's virgin pallet! Ah, my son,
My Andrea, we're buried from her breast,
Dead both of us, murder'd for modesty;
And when with fasts I strive to purge myself
From mem'ry of my manhood's sweetest days,
I see thee lying in thy little tomb
And fall upon thy innocence to weep.
So easily
Thy breath was stopp'd. Thou liest in the arms
Of Death, thy foster-nurse, mistaking her
For thine own mother. One may kill a babe;
But never curb the pulses of a man
To a priest's ambling pace. Veronica,
So cold, so hard thou think'st me, and I burn.
I must away where women are not heard;
Their silver voices at confessional
Thrill me like music. I must take the cowl,
Be where rough, angular, begrimèd monks
Will make me loathe my own condition.
Meanwhile—
Oh, he has children at desire;
Yet when he found Veronica in hope
Of motherhood, he came with ashen face,
Told me to hide her in a nunnery,
He would provide a coffin for my child.
Nay more, he would forgive my treachery,
Promote me in the Church, when he had scourged
By private shame his dearer penitent,
Would haply right her—but he plays her false.
He'll work the ruin of her soul. O God,
Mete out to me the measure of Thy wrath
In purgatorial fires: singe not Thy dove,
For I who touch'd her silver plumes well know
They cannot tarnish: mix them with the wings
Of angels, Thou wilt lose them in the white;
Then turn Thy unappeasèd face on me.
I shall not weary of my punishment
So she escape. To-day I take the cowl.

div.head: Scene II.
div.stage: —A Chamber. Enter Celano, a miniature in his hand and a roll of parchment.

lg.l: Veronica,
Thou'lt write at my dictation words that doom
Thy dearest countryman; thou shalt be false
To every creature that thou lovest, ere
I pardon thy great treason with my name.
How I remember when I was a boy
I thought all Heaven's blue was in those eyes.
Had she been spotless, I had been her slave
Who am her subtle tyrant; yet no pain
I can inflict on her can touch the hurt
She wrought upon my nature. Here's the king,
Who thinks I work to pleasure him.
What news?
Those rolls of parchment—Markwald, my worst fears
Celano's searches have confirm'd; he's found
A document that tells the truth as frank
As witness under pressure of the screw,
Revealing all.
Then is the writing forged.
So I surmise; yet it may yield a clue;
My spies shall fathom it. Within a week
We'll sit in judgment on a ripe revolt,
We will discover all.
By honest means.
My lord, I like not subterfuge.
Although
You use a spy, your wife! What news through her
Of the Lord Admiral?
She's sick, retired.
Through Clare?
What! set a girl to wreck her love?
I'll not believe Margaritone's false;
You force the king against him.
If we thus
Suspect and harass, we shall make him vile.
I see you've no suspicion. Painful scenes
Must follow on this plot's discovery
I fain would spare you knowledge ...
Painful scenes!
If Iolante's self
Were brought before me as a traitor, I
Would doom her to a traitor's death, I swear,
Nor ever flinch. What angers me is this:
You put disloyal thoughts in simple heads.
The people here are happy in the thought
Of keeping festival with their good king;
Celano, rack your brains to give them sport.
Spy on the revels, and no deed of blood
Will need your censorship.
Will you appoint,
My liege, when I of southern treachery
Bring proof, this fearless and impartial judge,
The uncorrupted Markwald, to assign
The several punishments
To the discover'd wretches: misery
Will be enough to me in leading them
Into their toils: let Markwald seal their doom.
Markwald shall be our grand justiciary.
I will: Celano, use you lawful means;
See I condemn you not for stirring up
Sedition.
See you have not to condemn
Those you hold dearest to you. Have a care.

div.head: Scene III.
div.stage: —An Ante-chamber to a large Ball-room in Celano's House. Celano, exquisitely attired, watches from a distance the dancers. Veronica passes.

lg.l: What a flower she is, a balsam! We are each masters in the art of winning men's souls—I to perdition, she to a fool's paradise! She thinks to bring me to her feet a victim; she shall lie at mine; though the landscape be fair, that to a conqueror's eye means desolation. I'll change the face of that fair country her body;—no respite till ruin bring her to subjection. She's dancing with Margarito; I like not the dominance of that grasp. Should he win her, I were baulked. Now he's offering her jasmine; that jasmine she shall tread under foot before sunrise.
My lord!

“The lady who calls herself your wife brought to me two days ago her babe for baptism. The attendants who followed her report, as I suspect to order, that they found her asleep under a cactus, a snake coiled about her loins. I send you your son, having performed for him the rites of the Church, in the charge of a young woman Madeleine, who claims to be, by your authority, his nurse.”
It's perfect. I secure her
Weary now, warm and a little love-faint! The room clears. The adieus! Does Margarito stoop low to smell the jasmine that his lips bend over it? He's gone.
This to the lady. Bring her back.
You've been dancing with a traitor.
You mistake;
I danced with you; and the Lord Admiral
For pity: there are dark lines round his eyes
For Iolante; wherefore is she gone?
Faugh! How that jasmine-tuft infects the air!
Unloose it; trample it beneath your foot.
Obedience! your toilet I will make.
I hate the dull, white stars.
How exquisite
Your sense of fitness; it's a wither'd flow'r,
And gives a look of tire and negligence
To one unweary.
Here's a brooch for you;
An amethyst best sets those moon-white breasts.
Now I can speak with you, I say, “Beware
The pestilence that walks in darkness.” Think;
One least speck of disloyalty would doom
Your body to the dead-house.
Sure, the wine
Hath wrought upon you. Never had the king
A smoother front. All's well.
This pocketful
Of letters will condemn the Admiral
To death—and the Archbishop.
They are forged!
Well guess'd, fair Casuistry. The ink is wet
Wherewith I penn'd them. I have left a page
For you to fill.
What mean you?
This: I need
Your writing—just the witness of your hand.
Write a few lines of warning—let them speak
Of loyalty—to Margarito. That
You will not do? I bid you think again.
Never!
The lover of the German girl
Is dear to you. You've seen two German maids
Preferred before you—Madeleine and Clare.
My lord is over-wearied, and his wits
Do him dis-service. I will take my leave.
You scorn such rivals, but Azaire held sway
Over Celano's heart and—do not turn
From sweet blanch'd rose to snowdrop—and Azaire
Is dead. This is no forgery. To-night
The Court shall hear of it. Veronica,
If with those clear eyes you look'd up to me
And said this matter'd not, the words were forged.
Be not a perjurer.
You're keeping me
Unduly for a guest.
With lover's trust
I'm treating you: to-morrow I depart
In haste to my wife's funeral. You can
Report to Margarito all I've said
Before the feast when I present the king
With these forged letters. You will not do this!
If implicated in this plot you ne'er
Can be Celano's bride, who—how you shake!—
Aspires to the high honour of your hand.
All know this ring; wear it as my betroth'd.
On what conditions?
Simply write a note
To Margarito; warn him 'gainst revolt.
Say that the Germans seek Sicilia's good,
And those are traitors who defeat their ends.
So I have ever thought; I would not stir
In any foolish rising. You exact
No more of me than this—I take the ring
And with it on my finger pen the words
Of your dictation.
'Tis to exculpate
You from participation in the crime;
And if I find you faithful, instantly,
When Sicily is humbled, as reward
For the better part you've chosen, you shall be
Led to the priest.

sp.speaker: Veronica
sp.stage: [looking at the ring and kissing it].

lg.l: The gem is exquisite.
I've seen you watch it flash across my hand,
With envy—half-contempt: tho' smooth enough,
My hands have not that rare transparency
That makes flesh spiritual enough for these
Moon-opals. Are you proud?
Vain-glorious
As you are of your will. Farewell, my lord.

div.stage: [Gives him her jewelled hand to kiss. Exit.

lg.l: Country and lover yields she to her lust
Of pow'r. I have the strategist's delight
In circumventing her; how great her fall!
Azaire, cup-bearer of the wine of life—
Azaire—she loved me for my handsome curls
And smiling lips, loved me as man, and I
Made her my wife therefore—while Madeleine—
She is my slave. Veronica! Oh, I
Reserve for her a place.
Bring me my boy.
The baby sleeps.
'Tis a sign'd picture, this;
Myself new-wrought in flesh. My fatherhood
Is past suspicion; these dark lashes hide
Haply his mother's eyes. Ah, keep them closed!
The child is well! Now, Madeleine, you know
What, as a sign of the respect I bear
To you, as faithful servant of my will,
I hold your due.
My lord, it is enough
That I may nurse the child.
'Tis not enough.
You shall be made his step-mother. You know
Of old we were betroth'd. A priest is here
To make the marriage firm. I may not vex
The king with private matters; for the nonce
You shall have rooms and tendance for the child,
But not until you have full wedding-right
To rule as mistress o'er it. In a month
I promise you open acknowledgment.
Put off your terror. 'Tis not to the rack
I'm leading you. Why here upon your neck
Is the little band of peach-stones that I set
Under the crucifix. Poor child, I've made
Your love a cross to you. But you consent,
Good Madeleine, to be my lawful wife?
My lord, you are betroth'd to me. I do
No wrong to poor Azaire, if I comply.
The priest will meet us in the chapel. Come.

div.head: Scene IV.
div.stage: —Room in Margarito's House. Enter Margarito and the Archbishop of Salerno.

lg.l: There must be secrecy.
My lord, not a feather in our plumes must be dashed, not a tongue shall be padded, our horses' hoofs shall clink on the stones and our voices be heard through the open casement to the last.

sp.speaker: Archbishop.

lg.l: I, as it were in a reverie, will look round. Con you the names on the scroll

That ringing voice is for a rouse. If the hen clucks she's not on her nest hatching treason. All the same I'll spy. Ah, a wedding! They were marrying and giving in marriage till the last day. Tessa, my child!

sp.stage: [A Servant-maiden appears at a chamber window.]

lg.l: A troop of soldiers! One looks up, he marks the house; he winks.
My lord, you've a waiting-woman would kiss a fool. Think you not the race should be celibate? Indeed, 'tis probable Holy Church forbids fatherhood to the priest lest he perpetuate folly.
My knave, what see'st thou, whom seekest thou?
What see I? Tessa gaping at the bride. Get in and chide her, holy father. ... And yet more distinctly I see the doves on the housetop.
Do not stare so at the house. Have you business here?
Aye, with the Lord Margarito; a fool has always business with lovers, for their whole business is fooling.
Pass in, pass in; do not whistle. There! On tip-toe!
News From my love!
And a kingdom must wait a lover's leisure! See how his long fingers dally with the seal.
Break it! 'Tis the light heart of woman, dry and brittle; 'twill not bleed.

sp.speaker: Margarito

lg.l: She's gone, my lady Iolante.
The rare Teuton wench denies me the light of her eyes

sp.stage: [carelessly handing the letter to the Archbishop.] [To Fool.]

lg.l: Go.
I've none to play with now the little prince is cowled and looks at the free birds as he strings his pater-nosters.
Tessa's a fairer toy
The very blink
Of traitors in their eyes.—God prosper you;
Prosper you—
How now? What is 't thou dost say?

sp.speaker: Fool
sp.l: Nothing but “God be with you, gentlemen.”

sp.speaker: Archbishop
sp.p: “Iolante and I have retired to my brother's villa by the bay, for Iolante is sick and wearied of the Court, and I am ordered to accompany her. See we be not too lonely.” That's near the convent where the boy is hidden. The monks are all Sicilian and true to their royal novice—save the German abbot.

sp.speaker: Margarito.
sp.p: I'll adventure it! A ride to the monastery, a secret meeting with my hooded countrymen, and the child is mine. I'll take him to the caves by the sea, and the lady Iolante shall receive him in her lonely villa. She'll keep the prince till we come to possess him of his royalties—and I pay a visit to my love! Thou art fervid for thy country; 'tis by chance thou favourest a lover's zeal.

sp.speaker: Archbishop.
sp.p: How sayest thou? Pour out our plans with thy love-sighs! I'll not consent.

sp.speaker: Margarito.
sp.p: She'll cleave to me as my ring to her finger. Well, my lord archbishop, all is ready. The fleet is mine; every ruddy sail flaps to Sicilian air, and feels the thrill of its freedom. The gates are in the hands of the Germans; but here's a key Sicilians can use. This scroll contains all names of note in the land, and they are all sworn to our enterprise. The prince I secure; Iolante keeps him. So our enemies will search the convent in vain. The child stole away from his prayers; would not suffer discipline and made escape through a cleft in the wall: the brethren shall be dolorously searching for him when the creatures of the Emperor arrive. We are safe. Look not so mournful. 'Tis thy manner. The owl smiles not though the weather shines. Thou art haughty before the people; show thy pride in the face of thy fears.

sp.speaker: Archbishop.
sp.p: Go to thy ships. The cathedral bell is calling for vespers and the holy feast approaches.

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: —The Garden before Veronica's House: moonlight. Veronica and Margarito on a terrace overlooking the landscape.

lg.l: Fair lady, we have memories;—that day
We gather'd figs 'neath the caruba-tree,
Gathering and giving—therefore I am come
To bid farewell, before I ride to-night
In chase of the little cruel recreant love
Deserting me. You're right; the moon shines fair,
Thrown as a bridal-veil across the land.
Do you love
Your land, Veronica?
Look at that peace,
The trellis'd gold of the vines, the lucid hills,
Those peasants singing as they saunter home.
I think
The moonlight comes that we may see our land
Lying asleep. Look, Margarito, look!
I feel her breath
On my brow,—Sicilia's breath! So sweet a slave
Chain'd to the ravisher? I am a man;
That sight unsheathes my sword.
My patriot!

div.stage: [Pressing back his sword into the scabbard.

lg.l: You'd spare your country's enemies?
I'd spare
Virgilia and her goats; those fishermen
Toiling at sea; the simple peasant wives
Who laugh even at their prayers—
And would not cry
If widow'd by the Teuton.
Just beyond
That light-irradiated chasm rests
Iolante ... and your love.
You mean my love,
The Lady Iolante! Fare you well.
How hard I'm getting! I can see him go,
And so I could to the headsman. I am hard;
I'm growing worthy of Celano's bride.
How the jewel flashes! I have kept it hid.

div.head: Scene II.
div.stage: —A Room in the Villa. Iolante and Clara at work.

lg.l: I'm tired of stitching daisies, and you sit
Like Nature at her meadows. Well-a-day,
Good Sis, I've little patience! Hark, who raps?
I'd greet a mouse.
The trusty coxcomb there
Alone may give his letter to your hand.
Worthy obedience! My servant's tongue
Improves your virtue serving it with taunts,
As bitter herbs give relish to our meat.
You shall be entertain'd.
Good mistress—no,
I must not tarry.
Take him to the gate.
Put down your work. Would you be glad to see
Your love to-night?
I never loved him so
As when he walk'd with me, here in the fields.
It seem'd to me, tho' I'm a simple girl,
He had that trust in me that Markwald shows
To you—his wife. I care not to be teased
And play'd with as some girls.
And you were proud?
Yes—of his trust.
And worthy of it, Clare?
Try me.
I will. Read this:—

“Gracious and beloved Iolante, Your prince asks pity. Can you withhold that milk of the heart from your country's orphan? His hiding-place must not be known—I have chosen the low caves. Bring Clare with you. I can trust my love. I await you at sunset.
Margarito.”
I cannot go. Why did you let me hear
Of such a thing?—Treason!
You will not come?
You've no response to that? False girl!
False wife!
Markwald, my lord!—and, oh, Sicilia!
And more than that a prince, and fugitive!
Have others then no country and no bonds?
If you forget your duty as a wife
To gratify a young compatriot,
Despise me not that simply I renounce
A lover rather than forget my blood
And all it binds me to. Beyond all this,
I'm Markwald's sister, think before you thus
Betray him.
I have thought: for in our life's
Most sudden tempest there's the lightning-flash,—
Torch of an instant!—all is seen and judged.
I'll not betray my country; and my lord,
My noble husband, will not be betray'd
If to his wife I'm true.—You will not come.
A trust, remember. Do you love him, Clare?
You then forget!
I see you will not come;
You're sewing.
'Tis a plot. That's treachery.
I will not keep a traitor's confidence
That is a snare under my people's feet.
I'll write and send my German page to town;
Sunset will not be here for seven hours.
These letters state the bargain which my brain
Hath struck with greedy Death—the written bonds
That pledge full many lives to sudden tombs.
Let's see! I read elated.—Markwald comes
With knotted brow. He fears your subtility.
He's for the battle-axe and honesty,
No toils, no snares, no scaffold.
How now, Mark?
I have a paper—to be read aloud—
'Tis from my sister—says: “This very eve
William and Margarito seek the cave
Under our pines. Arrest them.”
Noble lass!
Why look you so aghasted? We will find
Among our Dukes a nobler groom by far
Than this vile Admiral.
Who's written this?
The Lady Iolante without doubt
Knew of the secret and ...
The hand is Clare's.
I'm not a man for motives and surmise—
Absolute blank, where I can learn no facts.
And I beseech you, Sire, by all my sword
Hath wrought for you, and by my loyalty
Mine and my sister's, you impute no ill
Where you can have no knowledge. I myself
Arrest the traitors.
You! Oh, pardon me.
You are too heated. More, there is a pledge,
An oath ta'en you should be justiciary
In clearing off these treasons.
So I will.
Go, search my house—bring each to his account
Of all within. Do not let one be spared.
Oh!—Iolante, I shall be your judge.—
I must give orders. Lead me to my house.
Sybilla and her daughters are involved.
Let them be all confined.
Sybilla, Sire,
Sicken'd for death when we removed her child.
Doubtless the blow has stunn'd her; better leave
That agèd creature in her misery—
It's burning down to ash.
'Twill be rare sport
To stir the embers; the dull'd flames will hiss
And crackle fierce, I warrant. Hither!
Leave
The crownless woman to die undisturb'd.
No words for rebels.
None.
My heart is dead.
Peter, I like not this remorseful mood.

sp.speaker: Celano

lg.l: My brain may rest: no need of forgery.
In Clara's warning we've a real plot.
Yet will I make it seem that all along
I had instinctive knowledge of their schemes.
And this my painful scribbling

sp.stage: [putting back the letters in his breast]

lg.l: will avail
To humble my Veronica. I'll keep
These pretty running lines in which she's sold
Her birthright as Sicilian. She is mine:
The country I apportion her is Hell—
Confinement at my pleasure in its flames;
With just a hope across the gulf to catch
Sight of a paradise within my arms.
My lord, I must confess to you I feign'd
Creative faculty: for full four days
I have with diligence by piecemeal learnt
All that is here devised. This note confirms
My worst suspicions of Salerno's guilt.
I set your childish fool a spy to watch
The Archbishop, whom he hates for getting him
Whipt 'fore the Court; and he reports the two
Have constantly been closeted.—The lad

sp.stage: [The Emperor turns away with knitted brows.

lg.l: Will get revenged upon his enemy,
But lose his playmate in the pretty prince
He dotes on with a fool's capacity.
It takes much science to secure revenge
Without some personal discomfiture.
Salerno, Margarito, Markwald,—Sire,
You'll think I am suspicious—we must watch.
It's that old hag, Sybilla! Honest Mark
Against the charms of discrown'd royalty
Is scarcely proof; the boy must be immured
Deep in an Alpine fortress; for the rest,
Though he enrages me, I'll not withdraw
My faith in him; he's German to the bone,
As German as my fair Constantia here
Is rank Sicilian. Give us leave awhile.
I'll warn the guards and captains.
This revolt
I'll quell with iron heel within my house.
The Lady Iolante has of late
Been much about the Empress. Women here
Breed thoughts as they were men. I'll put her back
To her own woman's use.—How now! in tears?
You should not leave your rooms; your modesty
Keeps you a pris'ner till you give a prince
To me and to your country.
Sweet my lord,
I've given her a prince imperial
In you, and now, thus suppliant at your feet,
Beseech you look upon my woman-land,
Wild, ardent, dreaming, full of tenderness,
As if she were Constantia! Comfort her,
Assure her that the blood of her brave sons
By you shall be held sacred as the life,
Trembling within me, of your kingdom's heir.
Oh, pretty speeches! Have you practised them
Among your girls? Such cunning eloquence
Moves admiration. I will rule my wife
By German custom: you shall breed me babes
And wanton in the nursery: on days
Of state you shall ride with me round the town,
And what I will shall be your pleasure, if
It be to sack Palermo. Once for all
Leave policy and punishment to me.
You swore—
You promised me, if I would yield my rights
And be your wife, you would espouse my land
And cherish her.
Ha, ha! A pretty wit!
And I will keep my word. I govern you
As I will govern your Sicilian land,
Most absolutely—you're the stuff for it,
Fickle and tender and irresolute.
The stuff for making slaves! You've chosen me
A mother for your son.
To see him through
His teething, set him on his legs, as soon
As he can prattle I will tutor him.
You're for the swaddling clothes. ...
My liege, the lord
Celano urgently implores you give
Him instant conference.

sp.speaker: Emperor
sp.stage: [turning to Constantia, raising and hastily kissing her].

lg.l: Oh, then a kiss
And pardon.
I have cursed him on the lips.
Are men so mad to put into our hands
Such arms against them as I carry sheath'd
In my frail body's scabbard. I will bear
A prince to Sicily; he shall be great
And glorious the fervid southern way;
My own despised Sicilian he shall woo,
And as a bride be-jewel with his songs;
His court shall be the splendour of the world,
The sun of nations; men shall say of him,
“Constantia was unfaithful to her spouse;
He bears no impress of his German sire.”
Here, here, in closest privacy we'll hatch
Our treasons, my unborn avenger, here
Shall be conspiracy. Oh, I am weak
Even to the mortal hour, yet mightier
Than an earth-cov'ring host; for Motherhood,
That ancient Power with rights mysterious,
Won by fell Nature for her womankind,
Receives my injuries.
They're arming men;—
My child, we'll leave them to their battle-fields;
They may determine history; the fate
Of nations we will settle, thou and I.

div.head: Scene IV.
div.stage: —A Cave. Enter Margarito and Prince William.

lg.l: Boy, are you cold?
Why yes, my feet.
We'll walk.
Take care of the rough stones.
How dark it is!
So stiff and dark above our heads, I think
The ground that roofs our graves must look like that
When we are buried.
Nay, nay,—not at all.
The grave hath got no hole within its side.
It had one when they put the dead man in.
I've seen it—a black hole.
And this is blue—
With what the sexton sees when in a grave,
The sky! Cursed thought! I will not tell the boy—
Come, we will nearer to the entrance, so!
I like not stifling fumes of underground.
Lift me yon stone. Heroes have lifted such.
That's bravely tried!
Mother!
Where is my love?
She's no Sicilian; do not look for her.
Iolante, you reproach me!
You divorce
Me from my husband. It were easier
Refuse a newly-orphan'd babe the breast,
Than a sweet outcast prince my refuge-arms.
Yet, Margarito, yet I never had
One traitor thought. Why do you ruin me?
Oh, perfect image of Sicilia's self
Guarding her child! Why that is natural—
The cursèd German girl! Oh, the vile horde!
Now, my brave Markwald, were you here, that lie
Were back i' the speaker's throat. I'll keep the child,
Leave him to me.
You have no sympathy?
Do you not say “God-speed” nor even “Farewell.”
If Clare is false it may be all's betray'd;
This our last meeting. Iolante—Oh!—
Have you no “Addio”?
Heaven shield the right!
And me.—I am Sicilia's hope.
I feel
All's lost. Oh, Margarito, haste thee, fly
To Africa.—Thou hast unlawful thoughts.
There's some one coming.
I'll defend the child.
Lost! They are arm'd.
A show of innocence—
That child between them as a sword to make
Dolts of my eyes. Ah, I have driven snow
Over her wanton cheeks!—They're traitors all.
Advance!
Stand!
Never trust Sicilian tongue
He means no vain defence. Advance!
There cracks
One of thy heart-strings, Freedom!
Let me pass.
I'm wounded.
Yes.—Captain, secure them.—Come
With me. I would not have you manacled.
Markwald, the boy is innocent.
And you?
Am ready for my punishment. You must
Bear me away. I swoon.
Upon my soul,
Her innocence is twice the child's.
You taint
The wind, sir; not my ear. The prisons: on!

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: —Palermo. A Court of Justice. Enter Emperor, Markwald as Justiciary, Peter de Celano, Lords and Ladies, the Fool, the Archbishop of Salerno, Sybilla and her children, Iolante and Margarito attended.

lg.l: The court is open. This revolt had wrought
Destruction to our rule; ruin as swift
Fall on the workers' heads! Our loyalty
(That virtue gave Christ heart to be a King)
Is lost. You, proud Archbishop, have been proved
The root of this offence by witnesses
That my authority may not impugn;
And I condemn you to the death most meet
For such desert—
Oh, hang him by the leg!
His extreme haughtiness deserves reproof;
He'd suffer none before him.
Put him last.
Harness him to his courser's tail, and then,
Fool, his remains shall be thy heritage;
This the first property I've given thee.
I'd done the same by you, and may in Hell.
For Queen Sybilla, she hath done no wrong.
No: nor her daughters.
Do you mark that, sire?
He'd win a gentle sentence for the queen
To save his wife; he hesitates and doubts.
I note him: do not interpose.
Therefore
Let her remain in mild imprisonment
With her three daughters. For this kingdom's peace
Young William must be guarded; it may be
Prudent to keep him in an Alpine hold,
Where lawless rebels may not penetrate
To seize his person.
Oh, my lord turns pale!
He loves the boy: my Markwald, what he bears!
Too lenient! Mine the usurper's child!
And to no charge I'll yield him till he is
A prince no man will fight for. Take him out.
I will attend him.
See to her who faints.—
Sire, from his mother's sight to pluck the child
Thus roughly with such threat—
She does not faint.
Mark you her glaring eye.
My liege, the guilt
Lies not on that young head: it lies with those
Who harbour'd him. I do beseech you, spare
(You soon will be a father) the young prince.
I shall not ask you mitigate your wrath
When it lights true on the thrice-damnèd heads
Of Margaritone and ... my wife.
Ha, ha!
Celano, you judged wrong; let's wait to see
How a true Teuton tramples down his heart
'Neath the mail'd heel of his conscience.—For the boy,
He's mine to crush.
If you would shed his blood
In my sight, that were a boon. O God, I feel
The seeds of frenzy quick in me. Chains, chains
For the wild beasts at my brain! God, call them off!
I must keep wit for cursing. Lunacy
Will eunuch my revenge.
Give her a cell.
Keep in light bonds her daughters.
Now we pass
To other pris'ners. Margarito is
The arch-conspirator, and has seduced
A noble woman from her wifely faith.
Let the slow fire consume him!

sp.speaker: Margarito.

lg.l: Merciful,
To blazon forth my fate! I could not choose
Death more significant. I fain would speak
While the faggots pile; I have but two requests:—

sp.stage: [The Emperor takes the forged letters from Celano; they talk apart.]

lg.l: That my heart be given Clara, my betroth'd,—
The girl who set her country o'er her love—
Look for it in the ashes; it will throb
Laid in her faithful bosom. I applaud
Her action, tho' it dooms me to my pyre;
'Tis mated by her nobleness, who snapped
For her country even a more sacred tie,
And for Sicilia with rent bosom braved
Taint of a word that kills her as unchaste,
Iolante—
Let the fire consume your lips
For playing with that name! Leave me to doom
What of mine own is guilty. Lead him out
To the red stake.
Iolante, you must die.
Most willingly; bind me to that same pyre
We both have merited.
What, with him still!
Is torture sweet with him to share it? No.
You shall look on unhurt and see him die,
The next day suffer.
May I ask the block
For her? The bitterness of death is past
When she's seen the traitor blacken at the stake,
For whom she brought dishonour on my house.
Oh, it's a private grievance; never think
He'd send her to the block, but for the shame
Margaritone was her paramour.
Your private grief
Heal, cauterize at will: for us we'd give
Free pardon to so fair a miscreant.
Nay, we make intercession:—prison her,
After she's seen that fellow to his end,
And give her time for penitence.
She dies.
Iolante, will you speak? Have you requests?
My lord, you have done justly; I deserve,
As a state-culprit, death. Mar not your deed
By thought of private vengeance. Oh, believe,
You offer a pure victim to your God,
Or the sacrifice avails not.—Promise me
I may have burial in your vault, the place
That is my right: there, Markwald, you will come;
We shall be reconciled. You cannot bear
To be answer'd by a woman. I will lie
Quite still, and you will call me by that name,
Of which I have not lost the chrism-grace,
Wife—Iolante.
I dishonour not
My ancestry with a dissever'd head.
You shall not lie with them.
Then, sweet my lord,
Let Sicilia take my body as my life;
Her vilest ground is hallow'd. Fare ye well.
Clara will comfort you; she suffers most.
Don't tell her how Margaritone dies;
She'll think all's ended.—I am ready quite
To see the patriot lighted to his God;
He whom I love I leave in torture here;
My Markwald, Heaven grant you clearer sight!
Is the Court over?
The rebellion is
Methinks pluck'd up by the roots.
'Twas not to you
I spoke. Tear up those damnèd forgèd lies.
I thank my God they have condemn'd no man;
Each has confess'd his treason: thine the vil'st,
Who mix'd, dissembling, 'mong the wretched bands
Fooling and cozening them,—and thine escapes.
Softly, good Mark! Celano serves me well.
Iolante—
I've a boon to ask: none speak
That name: remind a bastard of his birth
Sooner than a dishonour'd man of her
He has miscall'd his wife. There's much to do;
The city is unquiet; I will set
A guard at the southern gate.
Nay, Markwald, take
Some rest!
What rest? Rest in the lonely grave
From which I've banished her? I'll keep the gate.

sp.speaker: Celano
sp.stage: [looking at Markwald, who is walking round it].

lg.l: The fires are dying down. What's blasted him?
Is it the bold of Heaven? Wounded pride?
He's built on Henry's favour. Good my Mark,
The Emp'ror shall disgrace you. God may scar,
The royal woodsman sunders you at base.
To-morrow, when my last great victim falls,
My wedding-day, the triumph were complete
Did not a rival's shadow cross the throne.
Peter, it's out! No Teuton can withstand
Sicilian arts! Markwald's been prowling round
That pyre to see
Justice on Henry's murderer?—the bones
Of a dead rival. He's for Tancred's line
Hot as was Margarito. There he stood
And blubber'd like a baby. I recall
His words, “The deed is devilish; you blind
The child, but not men's judgments, seeing eyes
Condemn your deed.”—I'd have such eyes put out.
Imperial policy. ...
Fool, are you crazed?
Is the Archbishop hanging by the leg?
It is not that. Lord Markwald set me on
To watch it all.—
The pretty lady Iolante stood
So white and cold against the flame. I ran
To play wi' the little prince, but others came
Gave him hot sport.
Your folly's lost its wits. Poor fool, you've miss'd
The jangle of your bells these last twelve hours.
I am a boy; master, be merciful.
You shall be whipt, till you cry out yourself
For mercy.
Get him flogg'd. A fool implores
